_comment: FRAGMENTS are the physical unit: a disjoint partition of one corpus build.
Every source belongs to exactly one fragment, so no byte of text exists in
two downloadable files. This is what keeps row ids safe to merge without
renumbering, and it is what stops a reader who installs 'Church Fathers'
and then 'Augustine of Hippo' from downloading Augustine twice.
COLLECTIONS are what the reader chooses: named, overlapping groupings that
reference fragments. A source can appear in as many collections as make
sense — Augustine is in 'Augustine of Hippo', 'Church Fathers' and
'Patristic era' — because a collection owns no text, only a list of
fragments. Installing one fetches the fragments not already present;
removing one drops only the fragments no other installed collection needs.
Adding a way to browse the corpus therefore costs a few lines here and no
Fragment selection is by tradition slug and/or exact author name; first
match wins, in declaration order. Anything unclaimed falls into 'core'.

collections.name: Creeds & Confessions
collections.description: What each tradition officially teaches: the ecumenical creeds, the canons of Trent, the Book of Concord, the Westminster standards, Heidelberg, Dordt, the Belgic Confession, the Thirty-Nine Articles and the Second London Baptist Confession. The smallest set that can answer a question comparing two traditions.

collections.name: Church Fathers
collections.description: The complete ante-Nicene and post-Nicene fathers — every patristic author in the library, from Clement of Rome to John of Damascus.

collections.name: Medieval Theology
collections.description: The scholastic era: Aquinas's Summa Theologiae, the systematic work that shaped Catholic theology and the arguments the Reformers answered.

collections.name: Ante-Nicene Writers
collections.description: The fathers who wrote before the Council of Nicaea in 325: Tertullian, Origen, Clement of Alexandria and their contemporaries.

collections.name: Nicene & Post-Nicene Writers
collections.description: The fathers of the fourth and fifth centuries, when the creeds took their final form: Athanasius, the Cappadocians, Ambrose, Chrysostom and Augustine.

collections.name: Thomas Aquinas
collections.description: The complete Summa Theologiae in English — all five parts, 611 questions and 3,115 articles, each with its objections, replies and the argument between them.

collections.name: Augustine of Hippo
collections.description: The Confessions, City of God, the anti-Pelagian and anti-Donatist works, the homilies and the letters.

collections.name: John Chrysostom
collections.description: The homilies and treatises, including the complete series on Matthew, John, Romans and the Pauline epistles.

collections.name: Tertullian
collections.description: The apologetic, doctrinal and moral works of the first major Latin theologian.

collections.name: Origen
collections.description: Against Celsus, De Principiis and the commentaries on John and Matthew.

collections.name: Athanasius
collections.description: On the Incarnation, the discourses against the Arians, and the festal letters.

collections.name: Gregory of Nyssa
collections.description: Against Eunomius, On the Making of Man, and On the Soul and the Resurrection.

collections.name: John Calvin
collections.description: The Institutes of the Christian Religion in Beveridge's translation, and Calvin's commentaries on the Old and New Testaments.

collections.name: Matthew Henry
collections.description: The unabridged Commentary on the Whole Bible, 1708-1710.

collections.name: Charles Spurgeon
collections.description: The New Park Street and Metropolitan Tabernacle sermons, and The Treasury of David.

collections.name: Jonathan Edwards
collections.description: Religious Affections, Freedom of the Will, and the sermons.

collections.name: Martin Luther
collections.description: Luther beyond the Book of Concord — the treatises, the Galatians commentary and the Table Talk.

collections.name: John Bunyan
collections.description: The Pilgrim's Progress, The Holy War, and Grace Abounding.

collections.name: Richard Baxter
collections.description: The Saints' Everlasting Rest and The Reformed Pastor.

collections.name: John Owen
collections.description: The Death of Death in the Death of Christ, Pneumatologia, Communion with God, the treatises on mortification, temptation and indwelling sin, and the sermons — thirty-one works from Goold's edition.

collections.name: Leo XIII
collections.description: All thirty encyclicals and letters of the Benziger collection: Rerum Novarum on labour and capital, Aeterni Patris on the study of Aquinas, Providentissimus Deus on scripture, Satis Cognitum on the unity of the Church, Immortale Dei on the Christian constitution of states, and the occasional letters with them.

collections.name: Catholic
collections.description: Trent's canons and decrees and the First Vatican Council's dogmatic constitutions — Dei Filius and Pastor Aeternus, including the definition of papal infallibility — with all thirty of Leo XIII's encyclicals and letters: Rerum Novarum on labour and capital, Aeterni Patris on Aquinas, Providentissimus Deus on scripture, Satis Cognitum on the unity of the Church. Aquinas's complete Summa and the Latin fathers the tradition rests on come with it. Vatican II and the Catechism are in copyright and are not here.

collections.name: Lutheran
collections.description: The Book of Concord — the Augsburg Confession and its Apology, the Smalcald Articles and Luther's catechisms.

collections.name: Reformed & Presbyterian
collections.description: The confessional standards — the Westminster Confession as ratified by the Scottish Parliament in 1690, the Westminster catechisms, the Heidelberg Catechism, the Canons of Dordt, the Belgic and the Scots Confession — and the divines who argued them out: Calvin's Institutes and commentaries, Owen, Edwards, Hodge, Matthew Henry, Baxter, Knox, Watson, Charnock, Manton, Flavel and Murray.

collections.name: Anglican
collections.description: The Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion, with Ryle on holiness and Matthew, William Law's Serious Call, Newton's Olney Hymns and Messiah, and Lightfoot's Apostolic Fathers. No liturgy: there is no proofread public-domain transcription of the 1662 Book of Common Prayer, so the tradition is here in its divines rather than in its worship.

collections.name: Baptist
collections.description: Both London Baptist Confessions — the First of 1644 and the Second of 1689, the central Baptist confessional document — with Spurgeon's complete sermons and The Treasury of David, Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress and Holy War, and Gill's Body of Divinity.

collections.name: Church of the East
collections.description: The branch that separated after Ephesus in 431, and the hardest of the seven to represent: almost nothing of it exists in English, out of copyright, and proofread. What is here is Badger's Nestorians and their Rituals, volume II — an Anglican chaplain's examination of the church's doctrine, arranged against the Thirty-Nine Articles, but built throughout out of long translated quotations from their own service books and from Abdisho bar Berika, whose creed it gives in full. The framing is Badger's, not the Church of the East's, and the source says so. Abdisho's own Book of the Pearl has no transcription anywhere that has been found.

collections.name: Eastern Orthodox
collections.description: Orthodox sources, together with the Greek fathers the tradition is grounded in.

collections.name: Oriental Orthodox
collections.description: The Tewahedo scriptural canon beyond the books shared with the West. 1 Enoch is scripture in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches, and is here on that basis rather than as a curiosity.

collections.name: Anabaptist
collections.description: The Dordrecht Confession of 1632, article by article, and the complete works of Menno Simons — The True Christian Faith, the Reply to Gellius Faber, the Conversion, and the epistles — with van Braght's Martyrs Mirror, which after the Bible is the book Mennonite households actually held. The Schleitheim Confession is the one gap: no public-domain English transcription of it has been found.

collections.name: Quaker
collections.description: The Religious Society of Friends in its own words: Barclay's Apology, the journals of Fox and Woolman, Penn's No Cross, No Crown, and Sewel's history.

collections.name: Methodist & Wesleyan
collections.description: John Wesley's Sermons on Several Occasions (1771), with Adam Clarke on entire sanctification and Whitefield's sermons. Half a doctrinal standard: Methodism's standards are the Sermons and Wesley's Notes on the New Testament, and only the Sermons are here so far.

collections.name: Restorationist
collections.description: The Stone-Campbell movement in its two founding documents: Thomas Campbell's Declaration and Address of 1809, which argues that the Church of Christ on earth is essentially, intentionally and constitutionally one, and the Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery of 1804, in which a presbytery dissolves itself so its congregations might sink into union with the body of Christ at large. Alexander Campbell's The Christian System is not here: no public-domain transcription of it has been found.

collections.name: Moravian & Hussite
collections.description: Jan Hus's De Ecclesia, the treatise he was burned for in 1415, in David S. Schaff's translation — a century before Luther — and Comenius's Labyrinth of the World and the Paradise of the Heart, by the last bishop of the Unity of the Brethren, which is the Moravian Church's own predecessor. The Waldensians are the gap: their confession exists in English in Morland's history of 1658, which survives only as scans.

collections.name: Old Catholic
collections.description: The Declaration of Utrecht of 1889 — the eight articles agreed by the Old Catholic bishops, and still the doctrinal basis of the Union of Utrecht. Short, and complete. It rejects the Vatican decrees of 1870, which this library also holds in full.

collections.name: Holiness
collections.description: The movement in its antecedents, because its denominations arrived too late to be public domain. Wesley's A Plain Account of Christian Perfection states the doctrine the whole family formed around; Finney's Lectures on Revivals and Systematic Theology, Hannah Whitall Smith's The Christian's Secret of a Happy Life and The God of All Comfort, and Upham on Fénelon carry it into the nineteenth century. The Nazarene, Wesleyan, Free Methodist and Salvation Army standards are all twentieth-century and in copyright, and no better archive changes that.

collections.name: Pentecostal
collections.description: The confessional documents of two of the oldest Pentecostal denominations, printed while the movement was forming: the Discipline of the Pentecostal Holiness Church of 1917, whose Basis of Union states entire sanctification, the baptism of the Holy Ghost with speaking in tongues as its initial evidence, divine healing in the atonement and the premillennial second coming; and the Church of God's Book of Doctrines of 1922. Both survive only as scans, so both carry a measured account of their transcription — the 1917 Discipline corroborated word by word against a separate printing. Later statements, including the Assemblies of God's, are still in copyright.

collections.name: Adventist
collections.description: Ellen G. White, the movement's own foundational author, rather than an account of Adventism written by someone else. Four of the five Conflict of the Ages volumes — The Story of Prophets and Kings, The Desire of Ages, The Acts of the Apostles and The Great Controversy — with Steps to Christ. Patriarchs and Prophets, the first volume, has no CCEL edition and is not here.

collections.name: World English Bible
collections.description: A modern, readable public-domain translation, with the Deuterocanon. Updated from the American Standard Version.

collections.name: The Holy Bible: American Standard Version
collections.description: The 1901 American Standard Version — a formal, literal revision favoured for study. Public domain.

collections.name: Brenton's Septuagint
collections.description: The Greek Old Testament in Brenton's 1851 English translation — the Old Testament of the Orthodox churches, including the Deuterocanon.

collections.name: Douay-Rheims (Challoner)
collections.description: The traditional Catholic Bible in English, Challoner's revision of the Douay-Rheims, translated from the Latin Vulgate, with the Deuterocanon.
